speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Prime Minister (a) how many polling stations experienced technical issues with the electronic voter registration system during the 2023 Presidential Election; (b) whether cyber interference for the technical issues experienced has been ruled out; and (c) what is being done to (i) ensure that all who voted were correctly registered and (ii) prevent a repeat of situations where persons remember voting in the 2020 General Election but which names were not in the 2023 updated Registers of Electors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To achieve this, we have put in place a set of procedures that need to be complied with.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Upon the voter’s arrival at the polling station, the election official will verify his identity and eligibility to vote at the polling station, and then register the voter’s attendance via a hardcopy polling station register or the electronic registration system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Thereafter, the voter is directed to the ballot paper issuance counter.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The election official issuing the ballot paper is required, by law, to read out the name and voter serial number of a voter before the voter is issued a ballot paper.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This allows the polling agents to mark their copy of the register and provide an additional check to ensure that only eligible voters in the register for that polling station are individually issued with a ballot paper.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a result, when the votes are tallied for an election, we can be confident that the outcome is the one decided by the eligible voters for that election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: After the end of each election, ELD compiles the list of voters registered to have voted on Polling Day and compares them against the list of voters in the certified Registers of Electors for the election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Those who were not registered as having voted on Polling Day are included in the list of non-voters, which is published after each election for inspection.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The non-voter list contains the names of people who have not turned up to vote.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The vast majority of them did not vote either because they were not in Singapore or were ill on Polling Day.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For these cases, their names were not crossed out in the hardcopy polling registers as they did not turn up at the polling stations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: After each election, there would be a few voters who claimed that they had voted even though upon checking, their names were not crossed out in the hardcopy polling registers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Thus, in reply to Mr Pritam Singh’s question, prior to the introduction of electronic registration at General Election 2020 (GE2020), ELD encountered only a few cases of voters who were on the non-voter list who claimed that they had voted.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As can be seen, the non-voter list for GE2020 was much smaller, rather than bigger, than the two previous GEs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As per every election, ELD published the non-voter list for voters to verify about three months after GE2020.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This was publicised via a press release on 5 October 2020, which was covered by the mainstream media.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms He asked why a tally of the number of NRICs scanned and the number of votes cast after the last general election was not conducted as a first instance check.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Given the much lower number of non-voters for GE2020 compared to the two general elections before, ELD did not suspect that an unusual number of voters had not been recorded as registered.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Checking the registration figures at the end of Polling Day may also not be instructive – and this is because the process to ensure voting secrecy means that we will not be able to identify individual voters, including those who had not been registered accurately and would therefore be listed as non-voters in due course.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Furthermore, every voter receives only one ballot paper and the ballot boxes which contain all of the cast ballot papers are always in the custody of election officials, properly sealed, with polling and counting agents able to witness this process, and secured while in transit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ahead of Presidential Election 2023 (PE2023), ELD publicised that the revised Registers were available for inspection from 15 June 2023 and that the certified Registers which contains updated information from the inspection period were available for inspection from 21 July 2023.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These exercises were carried out to enable Singaporeans to check their details and restore their names to the Registers ahead of the election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Similar to previous exercises, there were very few who requested ELD to restore their names due to inaccuracy in the recording of their voting status in GE2020.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As such, ELD did not suspect that there were significant inaccuracies in the recording.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The list of non-voters had been opened for inspection shortly after the GE2020 and the public were reminded that the registers were available for inspection in June and July 2023 before the Writ for PE2023 was issued.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Voters need not wait for these periods, but are able to check their status in the registers all year round either through Voter Services on ELD’s website, at any of the over 100 community centres or clubs or by calling ELD.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, there remained some voters who did not check that their names were on the Registers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For context, this number averages one voter per polling station, which had an average of 2,400 registered voters in GE2020.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, this is about one voter per polling station with an average of 2,400 registered voters in GE2020.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Further, ELD’s analysis of the distribution of the affected voters showed that there is no pattern across the polling stations and that the 1,093 cases were distributed across more than 500 polling stations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is because the proper registration procedure may not have been followed for the affected voters, especially in some of the more crowded stations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A voter’s NRIC and poll card are first checked by election officials at the registration counter before the NRIC is scanned to register the voter.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When the NRIC of a voter is scanned by the barcode reader, an alert or "beep" sound will be emitted and a digital screen will flash an "OK" button, indicating that the voter data has been successfully captured in the system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At this point, the election official should tap the "OK" button to return to the registration screen so that the NRIC of the next voter can be scanned.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the NRIC of the next voter is scanned when the screen has not returned to the registration screen, the alert sound will still be emitted, as this indicates that the NRIC has been scanned.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a result, the registration of the affected voters was not captured.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Election officials need not press any button to return to the registration screen to register the next voter.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Therefore, the issue of non-captured registrations as a result of not pressing a button would no longer arise.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Dr Tan asked what is being done to ensure that all who voted were registered, and Dr Tan, Mr Singh and Mr Liang also asked what will be done to prevent a recurrence where those who had voted were inadvertently removed from the Registers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We thank Ms Ng Ling Ling for her suggestion.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Dr Tan asked about the number of polling stations that experienced technical issues with the electronic registration system during the recent PE2023.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There was no evidence that this was caused by cyber-attacks.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Instead, this could have been partly contributed by the surge in the volume of transactions during the morning peak, where about 52% of the total number of voters had already voted in the first four hours, compared to 32% in GE2020.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For PE2023, ELD had endeavoured to reduce queues and waiting times for the convenience of voters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The number of polling stations was increased by 15% to 1,264 stations, from the 1,097 stations in GE2020.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This reduced the average number of voters assigned to a polling station from about 2,400 voters in GE2020 to 2,150 voters in PE2023.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Each polling station also had more e-Registration devices than before, from between two and four devices each, proportionate to the number of voters in the polling stations, with an additional spare device each for contingency.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For reference, a polling station with only two e-Registration devices can process at least six voters per minute on average, which is a 50% higher throughput compared to manual registration which does so at the rate of an average of four voters per minute.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a result, by about 9.55 am, ELD had reported that queues had improved at most stations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We would also like to thank voters who had to queue longer during the morning of peak hours Polling Day for their patience and understanding.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The electronic Registration system seeks to reduce waiting times and automate attendance taking for the benefit of voters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: ELD will continue to enhance the system so that the registration data are captured swiftly and accurately.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I declare that I have a Clementi resident who remembered voting in 2020, but in 2023, found she was not on the Registers belatedly and she regrets not having had the chance to vote and choose her President at the ballot box that day.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I also have Clementi residents who saw how hard our election officials, how hard our public officers worked, and the heroic efforts made by our public officers when technical difficulties arose.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can I ask the Minister supplementary questions on what I will call the "3Rs": reliability, resilience, responsibility?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When an electronic registration system is tested, is it benchmarked for 100% accuracy in the tender requirements, at least as good as paper, if not better?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On resilience, can I ask ahead of the Presidential Election, was there a proper full-dress rehearsal, incorporating set-up, log-in, getting the terminals up and ready, and then, comprehensive load-testing beyond what would be the traditional expected loads, to stress test the system?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is because I have residents who have concerns about whether someday, there may be cyber interference and we know what advanced persistent threats are out there.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I note that the ELD website mentions "Your vote decides the future of Singapore".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How we design these systems also shapes the voting process as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can the Minister assure us that ELD will do its level best to learn from this and continue improving, in particular, contractor specifications, tender requirements, so that the situations like these can be avoided in future?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Yes, definitely, ELD will continue to improve just as per every election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will take in the debrief and feedback from all members of the public and also Members in this Chamber, and ELD will continue to seek to strive better, be it process wise or the technical issues that we face.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that is the third question that Dr Tan asked.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second one, on the issue of reliability, yes, indeed, ELD has specifications on the reliability standards.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And let me perhaps take this question a bit further to explain what we mean by "reliability standards".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The reliability of a system depends on a few parts and to answer the second question, all these were also stress tested.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, we have to make sure that the hardware is functioning well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, we have to make sure that the connectivity between the over 4,500 systems all around the island, is connected well and has certain redundancy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And third, we have to make sure that the software is also working fine.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second is that we have also checked that the hardware has worked well and it was not the main contributing factor to the slowness in the first few hours, the slowness that started at 8.30 am that lasted until about 10.00 am during Polling Day.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For all the polling stations, we had double redundancy to make sure that we did not rely on any particular network, and this was also stress tested during the run-up.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Prior to Polling Day itself, they conducted full-dress rehearsals with all the devices on, to check the connectivity and hardware issues; and they were satisfied that they were all in working condition.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: ELD, in the initial findings, has pretty much narrowed this down to a technical issue that has to do with the software.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And let me explain it in layman's terms as follows.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But there was one particular feature that perhaps, in hindsight, the technical officers could have looked deeper into.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And that is when all the devices were sending messages to the central server and when the inordinate amount of surge happened, some of the messages did not get through.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And when the packets of messages did not get through, the system kept trying.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And because as the system kept trying, it continued to pile up a backlog of packets that have to be cleared.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, if you like, some messages did not get through, they continued to pile up, creating a backlog and it caused a bit of a cascade effect.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I must say, even with assurance about the redundancy, ELD's planning norms are such that in every polling station, even if the electronic registration systems failed, we will be able to clear the queues with the manual processes, as we had done in the past.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, the baseline is that manual processes will allow us to comfortably clear all the voters in that polling station.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On top of that, if this is supplemented by the electronic system, it will help us to speed up the clearance even faster.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister said in his reply that this number is now 1,093.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Based on the Minister's reply, will the ELD be sending letters and notifications to all non-voters in GE2020 who have not applied to put themselves back on the Registers of Electors to ensure that no voter has been struck off, due to the additional steps in the electronic registration system process that was employed in GE2020?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And now ELD is doing the reconciliation for PE2023.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will be sending all those in the non-voters list for PE2023 personal notifications, as I have explained, to encourage them to verify their status.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: That will minimise some of these problems that we have just talked about.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My second question is what is the purpose of this administrative step for those who did not vote in the last election, to apply for their names to be restored to the Registers?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Is this necessary or is the purpose still meaningful today, given that it can open up to potential operational slips and also additional administrative work for ELD and the voters as well, since they have to go and put their names back?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, is the purpose still a meaningful one?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Otherwise, he or she will no longer be able to vote in future elections, or to stand nominated as a candidate for elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In other words, the penalty for not voting and the process of expunging the names of non-voters, give effect to the notion of compulsory voting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Starting on a clean slate with no penalty will undermine this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Minister.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The first being, leaving aside secrecy, which of course we agree is very important, does ELD have data about how many total identity cards were scanned during GE2020 versus how many votes were eventually recorded as being cast during the election?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That would actually give us a first instance indication of whether there is any discrepancy beyond the 1,097 voters that have contacted ELD to say that they voted but their names were erroneously removed from the Register.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My second question is, I note that in a reply to one of my Parliamentary Questions in 2020, the Minister stated then that, in 2019 and 2016, one-off exercises were done to remind voters whose names were not on the Registers to ask them to take action and to re-apply to go back onto the Registers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am just wondering whether we can do a one-off sweep to all voters, including voters that were removed from the Registers prior to GE2020 and PE2023, to ask them to take action to put their names back on.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And also, in that vein, whether or not we can make it standard practice after every election that ELD would then send out a notice to voters who did not vote, asking them to apply, so that you do not just rely on press releases?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the end of every Polling Day, there will be a combination of electronic records in the current system plus some manual records.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because in instances where the electronic system malfunctions or fails for whatever reason, we will have to rely on the manual record.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, at the end of each Polling Day, we would not immediately have the numbers because there is the electronic dataset, which we have to reconcile with the manual set.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that is the answer to the first question.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And even if we can reconcile it immediately, it will not be able to tell us who are the non-voters accurately.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the second question, indeed, it is not so much about a one-time sweep or when the voters can check their names.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As I have explained in my reply, once the reconciliation is done, from that period until the next election when the Writ is issued, at any point in time, the voters can check their status.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we agree with you; we encourage all the voters to check their status anytime.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is not just only during the period when ELD publicises this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: ELD will of course still make the publications, but the voters can go to any of the community centres (CCs) or the ELD website to check their status.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On top of that, this time round, we are specifically adding this extra step whereby those who are in the non-voters list will be encouraged to go and check their status way ahead of the next election.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: To the Minister, just on my earlier supplementary question, the 200 and later on the number was revised to 1,093, these are individuals who got in touch with ELD to inform ELD that, "I am not on the list although I did vote in 2020".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My question is, again, based on your reply, the Minister said, following GE2020, there were 111,000 non-voters.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And then, from October 2020 to August 2023, 32,000 individuals applied to restore their names.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, this 32,000 would have to be a part of this 111,000 who were non-voters.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My point is there is possibly another 80,000 voters who, as of PE2023, could also be non-voters but who voted in GE2020?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I just want to confirm whether ELD is also going to reach out to everyone to ensure that they have not been erroneously struck off the voting list.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I hope the Minister got the subject matter of my first supplementary question.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The vast bulk of these non-voters, be it in GE2011, GE2015 or GE2020, were either overseas or some of them could be very old and very frail and so, did not vote.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For the 32,000 who asked to be restored, chances are that most of them were perhaps overseas or ill on that day and they have asked to be restored.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I do not think you will have 111,000 minus the 32,000 and, therefore, you end up with about 79,000 persons who have voted.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That would not happen because, from the numbers, you will know that this is not the case.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Also, from the previous experience, we know that the number of people who are so-called registered wrongly is not in that order of magnitude.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Perhaps, I should explain, just to put aside any doubt that this has in any way affected the accuracy or validity of the results.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Of course, the first thing I must say is this – ELD will endeavour to make sure that we minimise the error to as close to zero as possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is very difficult because, whether it is the manual or electronic system, sometimes, there will be an error.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we will endeavour to make sure that this error is the minimum possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But just to give a bit of context as to what the error rate is like.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we look at our recent GE results, the closest contest, if I remember correctly, should be Potong Pasir in 2011.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is about 100-plus votes difference out of about 20,000 voters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that margin is about one in 200 or thereabouts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Maybe I was not clear about the so-called 80,000.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am not saying that in all the 80,000 cases, there would have been some mistake.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am just saying there could be some individuals who voted in GE2020, but they had not informed ELD yet, that is the group that I am concerned with.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just very quickly and continuing on what the Minister said towards the end about ELD, on the day the press release was sent, I dropped a note to ELD because I had members of the public who wrote to me about this problem – and I would just like to say that ELD replied on the same day and assured me that they were looking into the matter.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we do not rule out that there could be a few more who may have voted but may have recorded wrongly.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And going forward, we will always do this process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That means, all those on the non-voters' list, for whatever reason they are on the non-voters' list, we will send them an individual reminder, on top of the public service announcements that we have made.
